articles.title: Ganymede Extrait by Marc-Antoine Barrois
articles.excerpt: A darker, louder take on Ganymede: incense, myrrh, immortelle and serious staying power.
body: I finally got around to digging into Ganymede Extrait, the louder sibling of the already loud original, and damn, this thing comes in swinging. People online weren’t exaggerating. This juice is a tank.

I get hit with incense first. Dense. Smoky. Zero subtlety. The mandarin peeks through for a few seconds before it gets buried by myrrh. The immortelle kicks in fast and brings that unmistakable herbal spice. Some people call it curry. I get why. It doesn’t smell like food, but it has that same sharpness that makes your brain go, ok, this is going to be a ride.

The whole thing feels darker than the original. Less spacey. More ritual chamber. You lose the airy mineral sparkle that made Ganymede famous. Instead, you get weight. Heat. Wood that feels almost metallic. It’s not pretty. It’s compelling.

Performance is wild. Two sprays and it clings to your shirt like it paid rent. I get why some people hate it. This is not office friendly. Not MRT friendly. Definitely not lift friendly. Wear this in crowded spaces and you’ll collect dirty looks.
But if you enjoy scents that make a statement, you’ll probably enjoy this one. It has presence. It has attitude. It doesn’t care if you like it. It just sits on your skin and does its thing.
Would I blind buy it? Maybe. But as a spice-and-incense monster with real personality, it hits the brief.
TL;DR: Ganymede Extrait feels like Ganymede after it joined a cult, meditated too long, and decided subtlety is for the weak.

articles.title: Lust in Paradise Extrait by Ex Nihilo
articles.excerpt: Lust in Paradise EDP is water color—translucent, sunlit, a wash of lychee and petalia over white cedar—then the Extrait is acrylic: same palette, but laid on thick, luminous and deliberate.
body: The Extrait announces itself with a sweet‑tart blackcurrant glaze, sharpened by pink pepper and a zing of red ginger. Rosyfolia threads a cool, petal‑fresh breeze through the top so the fruit never turns syrupy. It’s juicy, yes, but varnished—like fruit seen through a high‑gloss frame.

The heart doubles down on roses. Where the EDP floats peony and lychee in airy musk, the Extrait presses rose absolute and jasmine sambac forward until they feel almost tactile. Petalia stays in the mix, but here it acts like a fixative, giving the florals weight and a faint metallic sheen. It’s lush, a little clove‑tinged, and unapologetically “more.”

The dry‑down is where the Extrait shows its muscles. Akigalawood and cedar carve a clean, high‑pitched “rose‑stem” line, while ambrofix and musks lay a creamy, skin‑hugging base. The result is denser and more seductive than the original—less “Riviera breeze,” more “evening on warm skin.” Longevity is excellent; the first 40 minutes can be beastly, then it calms into a refined, persistent glow.

Performance is wild. Two sprays and it clings to your shirt like it paid rent. But if you enjoy scents that make a statement, you’ll probably enjoy this one. It has presence. It has attitude. It doesn’t care if you like it. It just sits on your skin and does its thing, loudly and beautifully.
TL;DR: Lust in Paradise Extrait feels like the original after a luxury spa weekend, a new wardrobe, and a firm decision that subtlety is overrated.
PS. Thank you Amaris for the Ex Nihilo Masterclass invitation.

articles.title: Midnight Espresso by Kilian Paris
articles.excerpt: Coffee, rum, chocolate and hazelnut give this amber gourmand the shape of an espresso martini rather than a straight cup of coffee.
body: Midnight Espresso makes its intention clear: this is coffee dressed for a night out. Kilian Paris frames it around an espresso martini, pairing coffee and rum with a heart of chocolate and hazelnut, then letting bourbon vanilla and benzoin settle into the base.

That progression points toward a rounded, sweet gourmand rather than a dry, freshly pulled espresso. The rum adds a cocktail-like warmth, while hazelnut and chocolate soften the coffee’s darker edge. It sounds more like the last drink of the evening than a morning pick-me-up.

For anyone who wants coffee to remain the centre of a fragrance, Midnight Espresso looks like the most direct choice of this trio. Its appeal will likely be strongest for fans of plush, dessert-leaning scents; those hoping for bitter roast or a crisp café atmosphere may find the surrounding sweetness just as prominent.

articles.title: Sparkling Royal by Kilian Paris
articles.excerpt: Mint and lemon lead into rose and blackcurrant, with tonka bean and musk giving this fruity floral its softer finish.
body: Sparkling Royal takes its cue from a Kir Royal. The official note story begins with mint and lemon, moves into rose and blackcurrant, then settles into tonka bean and soft musk. The result reads as a bright fruity floral with a polished, cocktail-hour frame.

The mint and citrus suggest lift at the opening, while blackcurrant gives the composition a darker, juicy centre. Rose keeps it recognisably floral; tonka and musk round off the sharper edges. Rather than leaning into a green, herbal style, the combination appears designed to feel lively and dressed up.

Of the three Cocktails fragrances, this is the one that sounds most suited to someone who wants fruit and florals with a little sparkle. The blackcurrant should give it more character than a simple fresh citrus scent, while the soft base keeps the profile from feeling like a fleeting aperitif.

articles.title: Piña Paraíso by Kilian Paris
articles.excerpt: Pineapple and rum open this floral gourmand, followed by coconut and frangipani, with vanilla and tonka in the lasting accord.
body: Piña Paraíso builds its profile around the familiar idea of a Piña Colada. Kilian Paris describes pineapple and rum in the opening, a creamy heart of coconut and frangipani, and a warm finish of bourbon vanilla and tonka bean.

The contrast is what gives the concept shape: bright fruit at the start, then a softer, more floral creaminess. Coconut and vanilla push it toward gourmand territory, while frangipani gives the composition a floral thread rather than leaving it as a literal drink accord.

This looks like the most sunlit and openly playful of the trio. It may appeal to anyone who enjoys creamy fruit fragrances and wants a clear coconut presence; those looking for a dry, tart pineapple or a restrained skin scent may find the richer cocktail direction more prominent.

articles.title: Heat by Akro
articles.excerpt: Red chili pepper gives Heat its identity, while cedarwood steers the idea toward a spicy, dry woody fragrance.
body: Heat takes a familiar spicy-woody structure and puts red chili pepper at the centre of the story. The note suggests a bright, piquant opening rather than a soft, rounded spice; cedarwood gives the composition a drier frame and keeps the idea grounded in woods.

That contrast is the point: chili brings the flash of heat, while cedar offers something calmer and more structured beneath it. The profile sounds direct and energetic, with the pepper note doing the talking instead of disappearing into a general warm-spice blend.

For anyone curious about pepper-forward fragrances, Heat looks like a clear, modern take on the theme. It should appeal to those who want spice with a woody finish, while anyone seeking a sweet or creamy scent may find its focus more brisk and sharp.

articles.title: Novae Vanilla by Atelier Des Ors
articles.excerpt: A mineral accord opens the composition before mimosa and blue vanilla lead into bourbon and Madagascar vanilla, amber woods and musk.
body: Novae Vanilla starts with an unexpected idea: mineral coolness set against vanilla’s familiar warmth. Atelier Des Ors builds the fragrance around that contrast, moving from a mineral accord into mimosa absolute and blue vanilla, then toward Bourbon and Madagascar vanilla with amber woods and musk.

Rather than presenting vanilla as a single sugary note, the structure gives it several textures to work with. Mimosa and the mineral opening suggest brightness; the two vanillas bring a fuller, softer centre; amber woods and musk give the base a warmer outline.

The result, as the notes describe it, is a vanilla composition with both cool and glowing facets. It may suit someone who enjoys gourmand warmth but wants a little air and contrast around it, rather than an uncomplicated dessert-like sweetness.
